runs.t: S1. The directory inventory and its coverage

text: S1. The directory inventory and its coverage

runs.t: The Colorado State Business Directory was published annually from 1871; the Denver Public Library has scanned 34 editions between 1871 and 1956 (1871, 1875, 1877–85, 1887–88, 1891–92, 1910–17, 1920, 1927, 1929, 1932–33, 1935, 1939, 1941, 1943, 1950, 1956). Every listing in the hazardous trades (smelting and refining, foundries, iron and steel and metal working, machine shops, chemicals and paints, petroleum and asphalt, tanneries, rendering and soap, gas works, plating, printing, plastics and rubber) was extracted by optical character recognition and keyword rules, checked by hand for Denver, and geocoded against a street grid built from the historical address ranges; listings with no usable street address are placed at the town centre and are excluded from all spatial analyses.

runs.t: The Directory of Colorado Manufacturers (Business Research Division, University of Colorado, 1961–2002) was scanned from library copies in 25 editions. Twelve of the scans stop part-way through the geographic section or have missing pages (1961, 1962, 1971, 1976, 1979, 1982, 1984, 1985, 1986, 1993, 1999, 2002) and are excluded from the inventory; the thirteen complete editions are 1965, 1966, 1967, 1968, 1970, 1973, 1974, 1977, 1980, 1983, 1988, 1990 and 1992. Listings were linked across editions when within 30 m of each other, giving one site per address with first and last years of listing. Against County Business Patterns the complete editions count 0.77–1.05 of the state's manufacturing establishments (1980 1.05, 1983 0.93, 1990 0.83, 1988 0.77) and correlate 0.85–0.88 with CBP across the 64 counties (log counts); the partial editions fall well below. For the 1880–1940 censuses the directory's hazardous-trade counts by county correlate 0.54–0.64 with the census of manufactures establishment counts.

runs.t: The IPUMS complete-count files give every person's enumeration district number but no address, and no public source maps the districts of 1900–1940. Brown University's Geographic Reference Files for Denver link household heads in each census to street addresses; these were geocoded with an offline geocoder against the historical street grid, and each district's polygon was drawn as the dissolved Voronoi cells of its geocoded addresses, clipped to the city. Districts with fewer than three geocoded households were merged with their neighbours. 73% of the 1900 population is placed at street level. For 1880, Brown's Urban Transition Historical GIS geocoded the census to buildings; the districts were rebuilt from those buildings by the same procedure so that all six censuses are constructed alike. The composition measures are population-weighted aggregates of the full count (race, Hispanic origin, nativity, year of immigration, occupation and Duncan socioeconomic index, tenure, rent, household relationship); only aggregates leave the project.

runs.t: S3. The 1925 zoning ordinance: classification and georeferencing

text: S3. The 1925 zoning ordinance: classification and georeferencing

runs.t: The Building Zone Map of February 1925 as revised to January 1929 (Denver Public Library, CG4314 .D4 G44 1929) is a monochrome print in which the thirteen districts are drawn as hatch patterns: Residence A blank, Residence B thin diagonal lines, Residence C cross-hatch, Residence D dots, Residence E thick diagonal lines, Business A–C solid black with a letter, Commercial A–C dense cross-hatch with a letter, Industrial A thick diagonal lines rising to the right, Industrial B thick diagonal lines falling to the right. The 11,849 × 12,000-pixel scan was thresholded, and for each pixel the fraction of dark pixels along short line segments in the four orientations was computed; averaging these over 32-pixel cells gives the density of rising-diagonal, falling-diagonal and horizontal/vertical ink and of isolated blobs. Cells were labelled Industrial where one diagonal orientation dominated and there were no horizontal/vertical lot lines (the industrial districts are drawn without block subdivision), Industrial B where the falling diagonal dominated, and Commercial where both diagonals were dense; a second rule labelled thick rising-diagonal hatch with lot lines as Industrial A, which cannot be told from Residence E and is flagged as uncertain (43% of industrial cells). After morphological cleaning and removal of components smaller than ten cells, the map yields 24.6 km² Industrial A, 3.8 km² Industrial B and 3.6 km² Commercial.

runs.t: Georeferencing used sixteen street intersections and park corners read off the scan, resolved to TIGER/Line road intersections; thirteen could be resolved and an affine fit in UTM zone 13N has a root-mean-square residual of 25 m (individual residuals 3–64 m, the largest at the City Park south-west corner). The 1944 revision of the same map (CG4314 .G44 1944) was registered to the 1929 scan with ten shared points (RMSE 25 scan pixels, about 32 m). It is a darker print of the same plate and the classifier cannot be calibrated across the two, but inspection of the registered Platte, Globeville, Sun Valley and Elyria districts shows the same industrial hatching in both, with the 1929–44 amendments confined to a few pencil-marked blocks.

runs.t: S4. Parcel matching and regulatory status

text: S4. Parcel matching and regulatory status

runs.t: Each geocoded Denver site was matched to the nearest City and County of Denver assessor parcel within 40 m (1,256 of 1,258 distinct coordinates; median distance 10 m). Where several parcels fall within the radius, as for condominium units sharing a footprint, the nearest is taken; the assessor's property class is the same across such units but the dwelling-unit count refers to one of them. Broad classes were assigned from the assessor's class text: residential (single-family, duplex, rowhouse, condominium, apartment, mixed-use residential), industrial and utility (industrial, warehouse, utility, railroad), commercial and office (commercial, office, retail, hotel, parking, service garage), vacant, park and open space (park, golf, cemetery, exempt open space), civic, school and health (exempt school, church, hospital, government, stadium, jail). Regulatory status was assigned from EPA's Facility Registry Service, TRI, SEMS and RCRA and from Colorado's voluntary-cleanup and environmental-covenant registers by location (40–75 m), address or name; a geocoding error of tens of metres can move a site across those thresholds, so a site with no match is a lead for records review rather than a finding, and absence from the searched inventories is not evidence that a site was never assessed or remediated.

runs.t: An interactive application accompanies the paper. It maps every site, pre-1960 trade, district, tract, HOLC area, 1925 zoning district and matched parcel behind the tables, with the same filters (directory years, sectors, regulatory status, location confidence) applied throughout, and provides the derived data for download: the geocoded listings by edition, the site inventory and firm histories, the district and tract panels, the 1929 zoning districts and their shares by HOLC area and tract, the boundary gaps and change models with their robustness columns, and the parcel matches. Microdata and address files from IPUMS and Brown University are not redistributed.
